## Summary

**Background.** Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) is increasingly
used to prevent graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) after allogeneic
haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), but may increase
infection risk. We examined its effect on survival, GVHD, and
infection.

**Methods.** We searched EMBASE, PubMed, and SCOPUS to April 30, 2026,
for studies comparing PTCy-based with alternative prophylaxis in adults
undergoing allo-HSCT. Comparisons were PTCy versus calcineurin inhibitor
(CNI)-based prophylaxis, versus anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG), and
between PTCy-based regimens. Outcomes were overall
survival (primary), non-relapse mortality, acute GVHD, CMV reactivation,
bloodstream infection (BSI), invasive fungal infection, and BK
virus–associated haemorrhagic cystitis (BK-HC), pooled by Bayesian
random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420261372156).

**Findings.** Of 4145 records, 247 studies (516 arms; 175 570 patients)
were included, 104 in the meta-analysis (9 295 in the primary survival
analysis). Versus CNI-based prophylaxis, PTCy was associated with lower
odds of death (OR 0·73, 95% credible interval 0·58–0·89) and grade
II–IV acute GVHD (0·58, 0·44–0·76). CMV reactivation was numerically
more frequent (OR 1·20, 0·87–1·65), particularly in studies published
from 2020 (1·43, 0·97–2·06). BSI (2·17, 0·86–4·39; four studies) and
invasive fungal infection (0·63, 0·19–2·44; six studies) did not
clearly differ. Versus ATG, survival numerically
favoured PTCy (0·75, 0·43–1·28) and CMV reactivation did not differ
(0·86, 0·51–1·42). BK-HC was increased against both CNI-based
prophylaxis (2·39, 1·41–3·73) and ATG (2·49, 1·08–6·24; three studies).
Publication-bias adjustment attenuated the survival and acute GVHD
benefits towards the null (0·97, 0·71–1·16 and 0·96, 0·57–1·38).
Certainty was very low for all outcomes except BK-HC versus CNI-based
prophylaxis (low).

**Interpretation.** PTCy was associated with less GVHD than CNI-based
prophylaxis. Survival benefit was not demonstrated: the association
weakened in hazard-ratio and bias-adjusted analyses. CMV and bacterial
infection were numerically increased. The CMV pattern fits T-cell
depletion depth; the similar BK-HC increase against both comparators
suggests a cyclophosphamide-specific effect. Close viral
monitoring is supported over avoidance of PTCy.

## Research in context

::: panel
### Evidence before this study

We searched PubMed, EMBASE, and SCOPUS from database inception to April
30, 2026, for systematic reviews and meta-analyses of post-transplant
cyclophosphamide (PTCy) in allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell
transplantation, using the terms "post-transplant cyclophosphamide" AND
("meta-analysis" OR "systematic review"), restricted to English-language
publications. We found ten comparative
meta-analyses, each including 6–30 studies. All examined survival and
graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), but only three pooled infection
outcomes, with few studies per infection and comparator. Where study
design was reported, the pooled evidence came mainly from retrospective
observational studies, with few randomised trials. None compared PTCy
with both calcineurin inhibitor
(CNI)-based and anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG)-based prophylaxis, so it
remained unclear whether infections seen with PTCy reflect the drug
itself or T-cell depletion in general.

### Added value of this study

This systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis (247 studies; 175 570
patients) jointly evaluated survival, GVHD, CMV reactivation, BK
virus–associated haemorrhagic cystitis, bloodstream infection, and
invasive fungal disease,
comparing PTCy with a less T-cell-depleting regimen (calcineurin
inhibitor plus methotrexate or mycophenolate) and a more depleting one
(ATG). The odds of CMV reactivation were higher with PTCy than with
CNI-based prophylaxis (odds ratio 1·20, 95% credible interval 0·87–1·65;
posterior probability of OR > 1, 0·88), whereas the estimate relative to
ATG favoured PTCy (OR 0·86, 95% CrI 0·51–1·42; posterior probability of
OR < 1, 0·74). This gradient is consistent with the comparators'
differing depth of T-cell depletion, although the credible interval for
the difference between comparisons was wide and included the null (ratio
of ORs 0·71, 95% CrI 0·41–1·20). By contrast, BK virus–associated
haemorrhagic cystitis was increased to a similar extent with PTCy
relative to both comparators (OR
2·39, 95% CrI 1·41–3·73 vs CNI-based prophylaxis; OR 2·49, 95% CrI
1·08–6·24 vs ATG). Estimates for bloodstream bacterial infection and
invasive fungal disease were imprecise and did not indicate a clear
difference against either comparator (OR 2·17, 95% CrI 0·86–4·39 and OR
0·63, 95% CrI 0·19–2·44), with sparse and heterogeneous evidence for
these outcomes.

### Implications of all the available evidence

PTCy is associated with less GVHD than CNI-based prophylaxis, but a
survival benefit has not been demonstrated: the lower odds of death in
the primary analysis (odds ratio 0·73) were not sustained when hazard
ratios were pooled (0·88, 0·66–1·14) or after publication-bias
adjustment (0·97, 0·71–1·16), and certainty of evidence is very low. Infection risks
differ by pathogen: CMV risk may follow the depth of T-cell depletion,
whereas BK virus risk may be specific to cyclophosphamide-induced
bladder mucosal injury. For clinicians, this argues for close CMV and BK virus monitoring and for
strategies that support immune recovery (optimised letermovir
prophylaxis, earlier tapering of immunosuppression, adoptive T-cell
therapy) rather than avoiding PTCy. Different PTCy-based regimens showed
no detectable differences, but with three to six studies per outcome
this is absence of evidence, not evidence of equivalence.
:::

## Introduction

Allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) is
potentially curative for many haematological malignancies, but
graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) remains a major cause of morbidity and
mortality after transplantation.[@zeiser2017] GVHD prophylaxis must
therefore strike a difficult balance: sufficient control of donor T
cells to prevent GVHD, without unduly delaying immune reconstitution,
weakening the graft-versus-leukaemia effect, or increasing
susceptibility to infection.

The introduction of post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) has
substantially changed this balance. Initially developed for
haploidentical transplantation, it enables
transplantation across HLA barriers and has made haploidentical donors a
widely available alternative when no matched donor
exists.[@odonnell2002; @luznik2008] Its use has since extended to
matched related and unrelated donors,[@kanakry2016] and in the BMT CTN
1703/1801 randomised controlled trial (RCT), PTCy-based prophylaxis was
superior to conventional calcineurin inhibitor (CNI)-based prophylaxis
for GVHD-free, relapse-free survival.[@bolanosmeade2023]

These benefits must be weighed against effects on immune recovery.
Cyclophosphamide given on days +3 and +4 preferentially eliminates the
proliferating alloreactive T cells responsible for GVHD,[@kanakry2013;
@wachsmuth2019] but may also slow recovery of pathogen-memory T
cells.[@zhao2022] This matters because viral, bacterial, and fungal
infections remain major causes of morbidity, non-relapse mortality, and
prolonged hospitalisation after allo-HSCT.[@styczynski2020]

Whether PTCy itself increases infection risk is uncertain. Compared with
CNI-based prophylaxis, CIBMTR registry studies have reported more
cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation[@goldsmith2021] and bacterial
bloodstream infection (BSI) with PTCy, with similar or fewer invasive
fungal infections (IFI).[@papanicolaou2024] These signals are
biologically plausible, but infection risk after transplantation is
dynamic and depends on donor type, conditioning intensity, graft source,
GVHD and its corticosteroid treatment, and antimicrobial prophylaxis;
infection risk associated with PTCy might therefore not reflect a direct
effect of cyclophosphamide.

The key clinical question is therefore whether the infection profile of
PTCy is specific to the drug or a "marker" of intensive T-cell depletion
in general. If the latter, similar infections would be expected with
other strongly T-cell-depleting regimens. If particular infections are
more frequent with PTCy irrespective of the depth of T-cell depletion, a
cyclophosphamide-specific effect becomes more likely. Comparing PTCy against both a less depleting comparator (CNI
plus methotrexate or mycophenolate) and a more depleting one
(anti-thymocyte globulin \[ATG\]) offers a way to separate these
explanations. No previous meta-analysis compared PTCy with both; each
included 6–30 studies and focused mainly on GVHD and survival rather
than infection.[@yu2019; @poonsombudlert2019; @gagelmann2019;
@arcuri2019; @gao2021; @arcuri2021; @tang2023; @luo2025; @jin2025;
@shahsavand2026]

We therefore performed a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of
PTCy-based GVHD prophylaxis in adults undergoing allo-HSCT, evaluating
survival, non-relapse mortality, GVHD, and infection outcomes across
three prespecified comparisons: PTCy versus CNI plus methotrexate or
mycophenolate, PTCy versus ATG, and different PTCy-based regimens.

## Methods

### Search strategy and selection criteria

This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance
with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered with PROSPERO
(CRD420261372156). We searched EMBASE, PubMed, and SCOPUS from database
inception to April 30, 2026 for studies comparing PTCy-based GVHD
prophylaxis with alternative regimens in adult (≥18 years) allo-HSCT
recipients. Searches were limited to English-language publications. The
complete search strategy is provided in the [appendix (pp
2–4)](appendix-preview.html#s1.-search-strategy). Reference lists of
included studies and relevant reviews were hand-searched.

Studies were eligible for pooling if they reported at least one
pre-specified outcome with extractable event counts (numerator and
denominator) for at least two arms differing in GVHD prophylaxis
strategy. Event counts derived from cumulative-incidence or
Kaplan–Meier estimates, rather than reported as observed counts, were
excluded from pooling (a protocol amendment, appendix S13). Single-arm
descriptive series were retained in the review for descriptive
tabulation only and were ineligible for pooling. Conference abstracts
were excluded. We defined three pre-specified comparisons: C1,
PTCy (with or without CNI or mycophenolate mofetil \[MMF\]) versus CNI
plus methotrexate (MTX) or MMF without ATG or T-cell depletion; C2, PTCy
versus ATG-based prophylaxis; and C3, within-PTCy regimen variants.

Two reviewers (MS and REL) screened titles, abstracts, and full-text
publications using the Covidence platform (www.covidence.org). Data from
PDF source files were extracted into a structured template ([appendix p
5](appendix-preview.html#s3.-characteristics-of-included-studies)) using
Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic, Inc.) with a purpose-built extraction script
(available at https://github.com/lewis-id-lab/ptcy-infection). All
extracted values were manually verified by both investigators against
source publications.
Risk of bias was assessed independently by two reviewers (MS and REL)
using ROBINS-I for observational studies and RoB 2 for RCTs, with
disagreements resolved by a third investigator (DPK). Studies sharing
patient cohorts were flagged and the most comprehensive publication was
designated as primary publication for each cohort–outcome combination.
All pooled estimates reported here were derived from this
cohort-deduplicated dataset, so that no publication contributed the same
patients more than once to any single outcome. The cohort overlap map
is provided in the [appendix (p
24)](appendix-preview.html#s12.-cohort-overlap).

### Outcomes

The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), analysed as all-cause
mortality (death as the event) at the reported timepoint. Secondary
outcomes included non-relapse mortality (NRM), acute GVHD grade II–IV
(at day +100), chronic GVHD (moderate to severe), CMV reactivation
(any), bloodstream infection (BSI; primary analysis culture-confirmed
bacterial BSI by day +100, with any-pathogen BSI examined as a
sensitivity analysis), invasive fungal infection (IFI, any),
relapse-related mortality (RRM), BK virus–associated haemorrhagic
cystitis (BK-HC), and infection-related mortality (IRM). Epstein–Barr
virus and human herpesvirus-6 infections were captured by the search
but not pooled, because case definitions, monitoring schedules, and
reporting were too inconsistent across studies to support a harmonised
analysis.

### Statistical analysis

We fitted Bayesian random-effects binomial-logistic regression models
using `brms` (version 2.23.0) with an `rstan` backend in R (version
4.6.0). The primary model (M1) estimated the PTCy treatment effect with
a random intercept and a random PTCy-effect slope for study, so that
pooled effects average over between-study heterogeneity in the treatment
effect. Each study contributed one pair of arms at a single timepoint
per outcome — the preferred timepoint where reported (day +100 or +180
for early outcomes, one year for late outcomes), otherwise the nearest
reported (fallback) timepoint — so no within-study correlation across
timepoints arises. An
indicator variable distinguished fallback from preferred timepoints.
Weakly informative priors were specified: N(0, 2·5) on fixed effects,
N(0, 1·5) on the intercept, and Student t(3, 0, 1) on the between-study
standard deviations (τ). Four chains of 4000 iterations (1000 warmup)
were run with `adapt_delta` = 0·95 (increased to 0·99 where divergent
transitions occurred). Convergence was assessed by R̂ and effective
sample size. Single-arm descriptive studies (n = 26) were retained for
the PRISMA flow diagram and descriptive tabulation only; because they
report no comparator arm, they contribute no outcome data to any
comparative model, all of which are restricted to studies reporting
event counts for both a PTCy and a non-PTCy arm. Arms receiving PTCy
together with anti-thymocyte globulin were classified as PTCy arms in
all three comparisons; a sensitivity analysis excluding the C2 studies
containing such arms is reported in appendix S9.

An exploratory steroid-adjustment model (M2), a post-hoc amendment to
the registered protocol (appendix S13), added arm-level systemic
corticosteroid exposure as a covariate. Because the covariate is
post-treatment and arm-level, and in most arms approximated from acute
GVHD incidence rather than directly reported, M2 estimates no indirect
effect and is reported only in the appendix (S9), together with its
definition, provenance, results, and a matched-set comparison against
M1.

Pre-specified sensitivity analyses included restriction to publications
from 2020 onward (a publication-year, not enrolment-era, subset,
spanning the letermovir-introduction period), to haploidentical-dominant
cohorts (≥50% haploidentical donors), and leave-one-out analysis. Hazard
ratios were not pooled in the primary analysis because most studies
reported only event counts or Kaplan–Meier estimates at fixed
timepoints; in a post-hoc sensitivity analysis, the reported
overall-survival hazard ratios (multivariable-adjusted where available,
one per study, direction harmonised to PTCy versus comparator with death
as the event) were pooled two-stage under a random-effects model
(appendix S9). Frequentist random-effects models (restricted maximum
likelihood \[REML\], `metafor` version 5.2.1) were fitted as concordance
checks. Publication bias was assessed using robust Bayesian
model-averaging (RoBMA). Certainty of evidence was assessed using the
GRADE framework adapted for observational evidence.

### Role of the funding source

There was no funding source for this study.

## Results

### Search results and study characteristics

The search identified 4145 records (EMBASE 2603, PubMed 1061, SCOPUS
481), of which 1220 were duplicates (@fig-prisma). After screening 2925
titles and abstracts, 517 articles were sought for full-text review; 52
could not be retrieved or were not in English. Of 465 full-text articles
assessed, 218 were excluded ([appendix pp
6–14](appendix-preview.html#s2.-studies-excluded-at-full-text-screening-n218)),
leaving 247 studies for the systematic review. Of these, 104 had sufficient details to contribute outcome data to the meta-analysis: 71
compared PTCy with CNI plus methotrexate (MTX) or mycophenolate mofetil
(MMF) (C1), 27 compared PTCy with ATG (C2), and 13 compared different
PTCy-based regimens (C3); seven studies contributed to more than one
comparison. Pooling was smaller still for individual outcomes: of 113
studies with paired-arm survival records, 29 contributed to the primary
overall-survival analysis after outcome-specific eligibility, timepoint
harmonisation, and cohort deduplication (per-outcome attrition in
appendix S12).

The 221 comparative studies included 511 treatment arms and 175 182
patients (@tbl-characteristics; 516 arms and 175 570 patients including
the 26 single-arm descriptive studies). Most were retrospective cohorts (129
\[58%\]) or registry studies (61 \[28%\]); only 14 (6%) were RCTs.
Median publication year was 2023 (IQR 2021–24) and median follow-up 26
months (22–36).

PTCy was used mostly in haploidentical transplantation (123 \[46%\] of
PTCy arms), whereas comparator arms were mostly matched unrelated (94
\[39%\]) or matched sibling (54 \[22%\]) donor transplants. This matters because donor type itself influences GVHD, infection, and survival; analyses addressing this imbalance are described below.

### Risk of bias

Of 207 comparative observational studies assessed with ROBINS-I, 141
(68%) were at serious and 66 (32%) at moderate risk of bias, mainly
because of confounding by donor type and conditioning intensity; none
was at low or critical risk ([appendix pp
15–17](appendix-preview.html#s5.-risk-of-bias)). Of the 14 RCTs
(assessed with RoB 2), 11 had some concerns, two were at high risk, and
one was at low risk. Concerns centred on outcomes requiring clinical judgement, such as GVHD grading and infection ascertainment (measurement-domain concerns in three trials), whereas objective outcomes (overall and relapse-related mortality, laboratory-confirmed BSI) were at low measurement risk in every trial.

### PTCy versus CNI plus MTX or MMF

#### Survival and GVHD

Compared with CNI plus MTX or MMF, PTCy was associated with better
overall survival (k = 29; odds ratio \[OR\] 0·73, 95% credible interval
\[CrI\] 0·58–0·89; @fig-os). Non-relapse mortality (NRM) showed a trend
towards benefit, but the estimate was uncertain (k = 11; 0·84,
0·48–1·28), and relapse-related mortality was modestly lower (k = 33;
0·86, 0·75–0·98). The effect on GVHD was more consistent: PTCy was
associated with less grade II–IV acute GVHD (k = 28; 0·58, 0·44–0·76)
and less moderate-to-severe chronic GVHD (k = 18; 0·41, 0·23–0·72).

#### Infections

CMV reactivation was more frequent with PTCy on average, but the credible
interval included no difference (k = 21; 1·20, 0·87–1·65; @fig-cmv). The
estimate was larger in studies published from 2020 onward (k = 16; 1·43,
0·97–2·06) and in haploidentical-dominant cohorts (k = 12; 1·34,
0·89–1·96). In the primary BSI analysis, restricted to culture-confirmed bacterial
infection by day +100, the odds were about twice as high with PTCy (k =
4; 2·17, 0·86–4·39), but with only four studies this estimate is
uncertain; no BSI model was possible for comparison 2. In the
any-pathogen BSI sensitivity analysis the estimate was attenuated and
uncertain (k = 6; 1·41, 0·56–3·03; appendix S9). BK virus–associated
haemorrhagic cystitis showed the clearest signal, and was the only
infection outcome whose credible interval excluded no difference (k =
11; 2·39, 1·41–3·73; @fig-infections). Invasive fungal infection did not clearly
differ (k = 6; 0·63, 0·19–2·44); the estimate rests on few studies with
extreme between-study variation (τ = 1·28). Infection-related mortality
was not increased with PTCy (k = 13; 1·02, 0·67–1·50).

### PTCy versus ATG

Fewer studies compared PTCy with ATG, so these estimates were associated
with less certainty. Overall survival favoured PTCy, but not conclusively (k = 6;
0·75, 0·43–1·28), as did acute GVHD (k = 7; 0·53, 0·23–1·17) and
relapse-related mortality (k = 10; 0·79, 0·55–1·03). NRM could not be
assessed because only two studies provided usable data. The infection
pattern differed from comparison 1: CMV reactivation did not differ
between PTCy and ATG (k = 12; 0·86, 0·51–1·42), nor did
infection-related mortality (k = 7; 0·98, 0·62–1·77). BK
virus–associated haemorrhagic cystitis was again higher with PTCy (k =
3; 2·49, 1·08–6·24), although this estimate rests on only three
studies.

### Different PTCy-based regimens

We found no clear differences between PTCy-based regimen variants for
overall survival (OR 1·05), NRM (0·55), acute GVHD (0·31), chronic GVHD
(0·60), or relapse-related mortality (0·78); all credible intervals
included no difference. With only three to six studies per outcome, this
reflects insufficient evidence to detect a difference, not evidence that
the regimens are equivalent.

### Sensitivity analyses

Full results are in appendix S9. The main findings were broadly unchanged in analyses addressing donor type and study design. Within individual studies, the proportion of
haploidentical donors differed little between arms (median difference
0), adjusting for this difference did not change any comparison 1
estimate, and restricting to studies with closely matched donor types
(difference ≤15 percentage points) strengthened rather than weakened the
survival association (k = 21; 0·58, 0·41–0·78). Trial-only analyses were
not possible, because no more than two trials per outcome reported
observed event counts; analyses restricted to observational studies gave
results similar to the main analysis (overall survival 0·79, 0·63–0·96,
k = 26; acute GVHD 0·59, 0·44–0·78, k = 27; chronic GVHD 0·48,
0·27–0·86, k = 14; NRM 0·91, 0·57–1·36, k = 10; CMV 1·01, 0·64–1·64, k =
7). Pooling the reported overall-survival hazard ratios, which were mostly multivariable-adjusted, gave a consistent but attenuated direction of effect
(hazard ratio 0·88, 0·66–1·14, k = 14; count-based OR in the same
studies 0·75, 0·57–0·93).

The survival association appeared stronger against CNI plus MTX (0·56,
0·34–0·84; k = 12) than against CNI plus MMF (1·10, 0·44–3·01; k = 5),
but a formal test did not confirm that the comparator backbone explains
this difference (ratio of ORs 1·82, 0·76–4·53). For CMV, restricting to
clinically significant infection rather than any reactivation gave an
estimate compatible with both a decrease and an increase (0·94,
0·49–1·71; k = 8), which does not establish that clinically significant
CMV infection is unaffected by PTCy. Adjusting for a letermovir
enrollment-era proxy did not change the CMV estimate (1·20, 0·86–1·67).
No arm in the 2020-onward subset had recorded letermovir use, and most
of these cohorts enrolled before or across the letermovir era, so the
larger recent estimate cannot be attributed to letermovir.

### Certainty of evidence

Certainty of evidence (GRADE) was very low for all prespecified outcomes
(@tbl-results; [appendix
S10–S11](appendix-preview.html#s11.-grade-certainty-of-evidence-profiles)),
mainly because of the predominance of observational studies, risk of
confounding, between-study inconsistency, and imprecision. Imprecision
was judged against clinically meaningful thresholds (OR 0·80 for
benefit, 1·25 for harm). Every prespecified outcome was downgraded for
imprecision except C1 acute GVHD, whose interval lay entirely below
0·80; this outcome was nevertheless rated very low because of
inconsistency and publication bias. Among secondary outcomes added by
protocol amendment, certainty was low for BK virus–associated
haemorrhagic cystitis versus
CNI-based prophylaxis and very low for the remainder (appendix S11).

Publication-bias analyses (robust Bayesian model-averaging) found strong
evidence of bias for both overall survival and acute GVHD in comparison
1 (Bayes factors for bias 10·4 and 10·9). After adjustment, both
estimates were close to no effect (overall survival 0·97, 0·71–1·16;
acute GVHD 0·96, 0·57–1·38; appendix S10), so the size of the unadjusted
benefits should be interpreted cautiously.

## Discussion

This systematic review and meta-analysis of 247 studies (516 treatment arms; over 175 000 patients) evaluated the benefits and infection risks of PTCy-based GVHD prophylaxis within a single analytic framework. Compared with CNI plus MTX or MMF, PTCy was associated with less acute and chronic GVHD and better overall survival, but also with signals for more CMV reactivation, bacterial BSI, and BK virus reactivation, which were generally less certain than the GVHD findings. Against ATG, the survival and GVHD advantages were smaller and more uncertain, and CMV reactivation was not increased. The infection profile of PTCy may therefore depend on both the comparator and the pathogen.

### Survival and GVHD

The reduction in GVHD is consistent with how PTCy works: given shortly
after transplantation, it targets the rapidly dividing donor T cells
responsible for alloreactivity.[@kanakry2013; @wachsmuth2019] In
comparison 1, PTCy was associated with about 108 fewer cases of grade
II–IV acute GVHD per 1000 patients (from a median comparator-arm
incidence of 33%) and about 68 fewer deaths per 1000 patients by one
year (from a median comparator-arm mortality of 35%). Better GVHD
control may reduce the need for prolonged immunosuppression and
corticosteroids, which contribute to both infection and non-relapse
mortality, as GVHD and its treatment are leading drivers of non-relapse
mortality.[@zeiser2017] An exploratory steroid-adjustment analysis
(appendix S9) was compatible with this pathway. This offers a plausible
explanation for how PTCy could be associated with better survival
despite concerns about infection. These findings are
consistent with the matched-donor result of BMT CTN
1703[@bolanosmeade2023] and extend across donor types, conditioning
regimens, and geographic settings, although the ATG comparison was
underpowered relative to comparison 1.

### CMV

The odds of CMV reactivation were about 20% higher with PTCy than with
CNI-based prophylaxis, with substantial uncertainty, but were not
increased compared with ATG. One explanation is that CMV risk follows
the depth of T-cell depletion rather than cyclophosphamide itself.
CNI-based prophylaxis, PTCy, and ATG deplete T cells to increasing
degrees, and impaired CMV-specific cellular immunity is a key
determinant of reactivation.[@zhao2022] However, our analysis cannot
prove this. A formal indirect comparison of the two pooled CMV
estimates did not resolve the difference (ratio of ORs 1·41 for C1
versus C2, 0·76–2·54), nor did a meta-regression on comparator class
pooling both datasets (k = 33; ratio of ORs 0·71 for C2 versus C1,
0·41–1·20; appendix S9). Moreover, the two comparisons enrolled
different populations (mainly haploidentical transplants in comparison
1, matched donors in comparison 2), so differences between them may
reflect the patient profile rather than the type of GVHD prophylaxis. The depletion-depth
ordering (CNI-based \< PTCy \< ATG) is therefore a hypothesis compatible
with the data, not a proven hierarchy. One external comparison supports
it: in a meta-analysis of haploidentical transplantation, CMV
reactivation was more frequent with combined ATG–PTCy than with PTCy
alone (risk ratio 1·42, 1·03–1·95) but similar to ATG alone (1·04,
0·74–1·45).[@luo2025]

### BK virus–associated haemorrhagic cystitis

BK virus–associated haemorrhagic cystitis showed a different pattern:
the increase was almost identical against CNI-based prophylaxis and ATG
(OR 2·39 *vs* 2·49; ratio 0·96, 0·33–2·50). This is compatible with a
cyclophosphamide-specific effect rather than a general effect of
T-cell depletion; cyclophosphamide is a recognised cause of
haemorrhagic cystitis, of which BK virus reactivation is a major
driver after allo-HSCT.[@kaphan2021; @ruggeri2015; @chorao2025]
However, cyclophosphamide also causes chemical (acrolein-mediated)
cystitis independently of BK virus, so where BK attribution was not
laboratory-confirmed some of the excess may reflect misattributed
chemical cystitis. With only three studies versus ATG and a
correspondingly influential prior, this interpretation is preliminary.

### Bacterial and fungal infections

The data suggest a possible increase in bacterial BSI with PTCy, but
with four studies the size of this risk cannot be established. There was
no convincing evidence that PTCy affects IFI. The few available studies
were highly heterogeneous, probably reflecting differences in antifungal
prophylaxis and fungal diagnostic strategies, and the estimate is
compatible with anything from a large reduction to a large increase. Importantly, infection-related mortality
was not increased.

### Balancing benefits and risks

For clinicians, PTCy should not be regarded simply as "higher-risk" or
"lower-risk" for infection. The data instead suggest a trade-off: better
GVHD control and possibly better survival, alongside greater
susceptibility to selected infections, particularly CMV and BK virus.
Absolute effects are more informative than ORs. At the median
comparator-arm rates, the CMV OR of 1·20 corresponds to about 46
additional reactivations per 1000 patients by day +100 (a relative risk
of about 1·09 at a 48% baseline), and refers to reactivation rather than
clinically significant disease. The BK-HC OR of 2·39 corresponds to
about 134 additional cases per 1000 patients from a 13% baseline,
although BK-HC definitions and screening varied between studies. These
findings support
careful CMV and BK virus monitoring in patients receiving PTCy,
appropriate antiviral prophylaxis such as letermovir,[@marty2017] and
pre-emptive treatment of clinically significant infection. They do not
justify avoiding PTCy because of infection concerns. Mitigation is more
likely to come from strategies that improve immune recovery, such as
effective CMV prophylaxis, earlier tapering of unnecessary
immunosuppression, and adoptive transfer of pathogen-specific T cells —
strategies not evaluated in this analysis and mentioned here as
hypotheses for future study.
The larger CMV estimate in recent publications remains unexplained: it
was not attributable to letermovir, and changes in patient populations,
surveillance, and reporting may have contributed.

### Reporting of infectious complications in allo-HSCT GVHD prophylaxis studies

Only 104 of the 247 included studies (42%) had sufficient information on
infectious complications for analysis, and inconsistencies in infection
reporting and definitions made data pooling more difficult. There is
clearly a need for a minimum core reporting dataset for infection events
in immunocompromised patients — covering category, site, severity,
organism, and endpoints — across all oncology study types. Standardised
reporting of infectious events and their attributable complications,
alongside improved diagnostic, treatment, and prevention approaches,
will strengthen future meta-analyses of pooled data.

Future studies should measure immune reconstitution alongside infection
outcomes to test whether delayed T-cell recovery explains the CMV
pattern.

### Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, most evidence was
observational; although sensitivity analyses were generally consistent,
residual confounding by donor type, conditioning intensity, transplant
platform, antimicrobial prophylaxis, diagnostic approaches, and
centre-specific variation in supportive care cannot be excluded. Second,
infection definitions varied (for example, any CMV reactivation versus
clinically significant infection; any positive blood culture versus BSI
requiring intensive care). Third, because of inconsistent reporting, no
information was available on the severity of infections at presentation
or on their subsequent course. Fourth, several estimates rest on few
studies (four for BSI, six for IFI, three for BK-HC versus ATG). With
so few studies, the data say very little about how much the true effect
varies between studies, so that part of the model is driven largely by
the chosen prior rather than the evidence; the credible intervals for
these sparse outcomes (six studies or fewer) are probably narrower than
they should be and are best read as a lower bound on the real
uncertainty. Fifth, IFI showed extreme heterogeneity, probably
reflecting antifungal prophylaxis, local epidemiology, and diagnostic
approaches. Sixth, cohort deduplication removed the largest registry publications from seven
outcomes where a smaller series reports the same patients in more
detail, so the survival and chronic GVHD analyses rest on fewer patients
than the size of the review suggests (appendix S12). Finally,
publication bias is a concern: the survival and acute GVHD benefits were
substantially attenuated after adjustment, so the magnitude of benefit
in the primary analysis should not be assumed to be the true treatment
effect. Similarly, the absence of differences between PTCy-based
regimens, with three to six studies per outcome, does not support
flexibility in dosing or backbone selection.

In conclusion, PTCy-based prophylaxis was associated with less acute and
chronic GVHD than CNI plus MTX or MMF. A survival benefit was not
demonstrated: the lower odds of death in the primary analysis did not
persist when hazard ratios were pooled or after publication-bias
adjustment, and the prediction interval was wide (0·29–1·82). This
evidence was predominantly observational, and the acute GVHD estimate
was also weakened by publication-bias adjustment.
The infection findings were pathogen-specific: PTCy was associated with
possible increases in CMV reactivation and bacterial BSI versus
CNI-based prophylaxis and with the most consistent increase in BK virus
reactivation, whereas CMV reactivation was not clearly increased versus
ATG. CMV risk may relate partly to the depth of T-cell depletion and the
BK signal to cyclophosphamide itself, but both remain hypotheses.
Overall, the evidence supports a benefit–risk trade-off rather than a
simple advantage or disadvantage. PTCy provides effective GVHD control,
and clinicians should
remain attentive to CMV and BK virus reactivation, and to a potential
excess of bacterial bloodstream infections.
Given the very low certainty of evidence, these findings are
hypothesis-generating and should inform, not replace, adequately powered
randomised trials.

REL, MS, and DPK developed the study protocol. REL and MS performed the
searches, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, and statistical
analysis, and MS wrote the first draft of the report. MS and REL
verified the extracted data. DPK revised the manuscript. All authors had
full access to all the data in the study and had final responsibility
for the decision to submit for publication.

## Data sharing

Individual study-level data extracted for this systematic review,
including the complete extraction database and analytic datasets, are
available on a public GitHub repository
<https://github.com/lewis-id-lab/ptcy-infection.git>. The manuscript
source, including the notebooks that generate every table and figure, is
available with a rendered version for review at
<https://lewis-id-lab.github.io/ptcy-infection/>. A permanent archive of
the repository release used for this analysis will be deposited on
Zenodo with a DOI at submission. The study protocol is registered with
PROSPERO (CRD420261372156).

## Use of artificial intelligence

AI tools (Claude Code, model Claude Opus 4.8; Anthropic, Inc.) were
used to aid data extraction from original PDF source documents into a
data collection form.
AI-extracted values were manually verified by the investigators against
source publications. Posit Assistant (Posit, Inc.) was used for R
statistical code debugging within the Positron integrated development
environment (IDE) during analysis. The authors take full
responsibility for the analysis and manuscript contents.

## Figures

![**Study selection (PRISMA 2020 flow diagram).** 4145 records were
identified from databases (EMBASE 2603, PubMed 1061, SCOPUS 481) and
1220 duplicates removed. 2925 records were screened and 2408 excluded at
title and abstract. 517 reports were sought for retrieval; 52 were not
retrieved or not in English (not recorded as separate counts). 465
full-text reports were assessed and 218 excluded ([appendix pp
6–14](appendix-preview.html#s2.-studies-excluded-at-full-text-screening-n218)).
247 studies were included in the systematic review; four publications
entered twice during extraction were removed (appendix
S12). 104 unique studies contributed outcome data to the meta-analysis
(C1 71 studies; C2 27 studies; C3 13 studies; 7 studies contribute to

more than one comparison). Reference lists, citation tracking, and
PROSPERO registrations were also searched but yielded no separately
recorded reports, so the identification-via-other-methods branch of the
diagram shows zero.](figures/Figure1_PRISMA_flow_diagram){#fig-prisma}

Bayesian random-effects posterior median with 95% credible interval
(primary model M1). Events and totals of each arm and REML
